d.title: The score matrix nobody wants to store
d.caption: Attention's inner `QKᵀ` is an n×n matrix of scores, and the standard implementation writes it to memory, reads it back for the softmax, writes the result, and reads it again for the final multiply. **The arithmetic is modest; the traffic is not.** At 16,384 tokens the scores across 32 layers come to 549.76 GB of round trips — which no accelerator has, so the matrix is streamed in and out of HBM four times over.

d.title: The fused kernel, measured — including the row that goes backwards
d.caption: FlashAttention is **exact**, not an approximation: tiling, kernel fusion, an online softmax and an IO-aware design that does *more* arithmetic to move fewer bytes. The measurement mostly agrees with the 2–4× claim at the lengths where it matters, and the 256-token row is worth leaving in: **0.67×, slower than naive**, because at short sequences the fusion overhead exceeds the traffic it saves. The gain is a function of length, not a constant.

d.title: Where 'decode is weight-bound' stops being true
d.caption: 3.1 established that decode is dominated by loading weights, and that is true at the context lengths most deployments run — and stops being true as context grows, because **the feed-forward work per token is constant while attention grows with the context**. At 128 tokens attention is 7.7% of the FLOPs; at 32,768 it is **95.5%**. Which is why the optimisations in this lesson matter at long context and are nearly irrelevant at short.

d.title: A sliding window bounds the cost instead of reducing it
d.caption: FlashAttention makes exact attention cheaper; a window makes it **less**. Each token attends only to the W nearest, so cost per token is capped at W rather than growing with n — and the saving is nothing at 2,048 and **97% at 131,072**. The trade is explicit and unlike FlashAttention's: information outside the window is unreachable in one layer, recoverable only through stacking, so this is an approximation with a quality question attached.

d.title: Throughput rises 5.2x; the per-request step gets 6.4x slower
d.caption: A decode step loads every weight to produce one token, and that load does not change when a second request joins — **the same weights, read once, now serve two tokens**. Which is why throughput climbs from 40.1 to 209.5 tokens/sec. The cost is in the second column: one request inside a batch of 32 sees a step **6.4× slower**, so its tokens arrive 6.4× further apart. On a GPU that factor is nearer 1.1×; this is a 4-thread CPU where the arithmetic saturates early, so the trade shown here is the pessimistic version of the same story.

d.title: Static batching wastes 68% of the machine on chat traffic
d.caption: Rows are processed in lockstep, so a request that wanted 12 tokens occupies its slot until the one that wanted 320 finishes. On a uniform workload that costs nothing; on chat traffic it costs most of the machine, because **output lengths are long-tailed** — many short answers and a few very long ones, which is exactly the distribution that maximises the gap between the mean and the maximum. Note the waste plateaus at 68.2%: past batch 16 the longest request already sets the length, so a bigger batch neither helps nor hurts.

d.title: One prefill stalls every active stream for 34 decode steps
d.caption: Prefill and decode compete for the same device. A decode step takes about 39 ms; prefilling a 512-token prompt takes 1,315 ms — so while that prefill runs, **every other stream pauses for the equivalent of 33.9 decode steps**. Chunked prefill splits the prompt into four pieces of 128 and runs a decode step between them: the prefill finishes slightly later and everybody else's tokens keep flowing. It is a **TPOT optimisation paid for with TTFT**, right on a service with many active streams and wrong on one with few.

d.title: Acceptance rate is a property of your traffic, not the model pair
d.caption: Acceptance rate is the fraction of drafted tokens the target agrees with, and everything else follows from it — so it is the number to measure first. The spread is the point: **0.625 on technical text and 0.208 on creative**, a factor of three on the same model pair. Creative text is where the draft model's distribution diverges most, which is exactly where speculation stops paying. An aggregate of 0.417 would hide both ends.

d.title: K cancels, and the condition is r > c
d.caption: Let `c` be a draft pass as a fraction of a target pass, `r` the acceptance rate, `K` the tokens drafted per round. A round costs `Kc + 1` target-pass-equivalents and yields `1 + rK` tokens, so the speedup is `(1 + rK) / (Kc + 1)`. Set that above 1 and **K cancels entirely**, leaving `r > c`: speculation pays if and only if the acceptance rate exceeds the draft's relative cost. K does not decide *whether* it pays — only how much.

nodes.label: K sets the size of the win

d.title: 1.13x at best, and slower at K=8
d.caption: The advertised figure for speculative decoding is 2–3×. Measured on this pair — gpt2 drafting for gpt2-medium, a size ratio of 2.85× — the best result is **1.13× at K=4**, and **K=8 is 0.71×, slower than not speculating at all**. The reason is §02's table: acceptance falls as K rises (0.650 at K=1 down to 0.231 at K=8), so the drafts get cheaper per token and far likelier to be thrown away. A 2.85× size ratio is simply not enough; the published numbers assume a much smaller draft.

d.title: The framework overhead everyone argues about is 0.01%
d.caption: Comparisons often open with request-handling overhead — Python against Rust, async against threads — so it is worth knowing the size of that term before weighing it. Measured across every non-model stage of a short request: tokenizing is 0.090 ms, detokenizing 0.029 ms, and the model is **99.99% of a 922.5 ms answer**. Which does not make frameworks equivalent; it means the differences between them are in scheduling, batching and cache management, not in the server's language.

d.title: Four frameworks, chosen by the constraint rather than a benchmark
d.caption: Each row names the constraint that makes one framework the answer. The second is the clearest trade: engine compilation buys the last 20–40%, and it is worth it **only** when the model is fixed, because otherwise you pay a rebuild every time you change models. The third is specific and easy to miss — on agent and multi-branch workloads the saving is in sharing cache across forks, which is a different win from throughput.
